summary: Defines an extension to RADIUS so it can support Digest Authentication, used by HTTP-style protocols such as SIP and HTTP. It lets a RADIUS server check digest credentials on behalf of another server. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When a web or phone server wants to check a password without seeing it, it can ask a central RADIUS server. This adds the messages needed for that.

subtitle: New RADIUS attributes let a web or SIP server hand HTTP Digest checks to a central RADIUS server.

tldr.problem: HTTP Digest is the standard way SIP and HTTP clients log in, but RADIUS had no way to carry a Digest login, so servers could not use a central RADIUS user database for it.
tldr.mechanism: Twenty new RADIUS attributes (types 103 to 122) carry the Digest directives from the HTTP-style server to the RADIUS server, which picks the nonce and does the digest calculation.
tldr.outcome: A SIP or HTTP server can act as a RADIUS client and defer Digest authentication to RADIUS. RFC 5090 obsoletes RFC 4590, mainly fixing errors in the attribute numbers and examples.

today: RFC 5090 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It replaces RFC 4590.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Needs Digest
sections.content:
HTTP Digest Authentication, defined in RFC 2617, was adapted for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). Digest has known weaknesses, and SIP defines other mechanisms such as TLS and S/MIME. Even so, Digest support is mandatory in SIP implementations and is the preferred way for a SIP user agent to authenticate itself to a proxy.

To simplify provisioning, the RFC wants this mechanism available in AAA protocols (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) such as RADIUS and Diameter. Existing RADIUS attributes do not fit: the RADIUS client never receives a password from the HTTP-style client, so User-Password cannot be used, and the CHAP attributes cannot be used because the CHAP algorithm is not compatible with HTTP Digest.

So RFC 5090 defines attributes that let the RADIUS server perform the digest calculation from RFC 2617. A companion document, RFC 4740, covers Digest in Diameter. The RFC calls any protocol that uses HTTP-like headers and HTTP Digest "HTTP-style"; HTTP and SIP are the examples.
sections.eli5: The doorman had no way to ask head office about a secret handshake, because head office only understood the old kinds of password slips. This RFC invents a new slip for it.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
Digest is a challenge-response scheme. A client sends a request with no credentials, the server answers with an error containing a nonce, and the client replies with a digest made from parts of the request, the nonce and a shared secret. The server repeats the calculation and compares.

With RADIUS, the HTTP-style server (B) also acts as the RADIUS client, or NAS, and the RADIUS server (C) holds the users. The RADIUS server generates the nonces. Generating them in the client would save a round trip but would bring security and operational problems, and some digest algorithms, such as AKA, would not work.

B asks C for a nonce with an Access-Request carrying Digest-Method and Digest-URI but no Digest-Nonce. C replies with an Access-Challenge. B turns that into a "(Proxy) Authorization required" response. When A comes back with credentials, B sends them in a second Access-Request, and C answers with Access-Accept or Access-Reject.
sections.eli5: The doorman phones head office, which makes up a fresh secret question. The visitor answers it, the doorman passes the answer along, and head office says yes or no.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
RADIUS client. It must send zero or exactly one credential set to the server, choosing the one whose realm matches its locally configured realm. If the nonce is recognized, it copies the header directives into matching Digest-* attributes and the request method into Digest-Method. It strips only the surrounding quotes and does not unescape anything. For qop auth-int it also hashes the entity body into Digest-Entity-Body-Hash. It adds a Message-Authenticator attribute.

On Access-Accept, the client builds an Authentication-Info header from Digest-Response-Auth, or from Digest-HA1 in the auth-int case when the algorithm is MD5-sess or AKAv1-MD5-sess, or when IPsec protects the RADIUS traffic. A Digest-Nextnonce value goes into the nextnonce directive. If the server did not accept the nonce, an Access-Challenge with Digest-Stale true leads to a 401 or 407 response with stale set.

RADIUS server. Without a nonce in the request, it issues one in an Access-Challenge, and it MUST include Digest-Realm and Message-Authenticator. With a Digest-Response it checks that mandatory attributes are present (MD5 is assumed if Digest-Algorithm is missing), that the client may serve the realm, and that the user may access the protection space and any SIP-AOR. Failures give Access-Reject. If the response matches but the nonce is too old, the reply is an Access-Challenge with a new nonce and Digest-Stale true.
sections.eli5: The doorman copies what the visitor said onto the slip without changing it. Head office checks the answer, checks the visitor is allowed in this club, and can say the question was too old and ask a fresh one.

sections.title: The New Attributes
sections.content:
Unless stated otherwise, each attribute has the usual RADIUS layout of Type, Length and a Text field. The RFC defines 20 attributes, with types 103 through 122. Examples include Digest-Response (103), which makes the server treat an Access-Request as a Digest request and holds a 32-octet hexadecimal value for HTTP Digest, and Digest-Nonce (105).

Each attribute is restricted to certain packets. Digest-Response-Auth (106) and Digest-Nextnonce (107) appear only in Access-Accept. Digest-Stale (120) appears only in Access-Challenge. Digest-HA1 (121) is sent only in Access-Accept, and then only for qop auth-int under the conditions above. SIP-AOR (122) is used when the client wants to authorize SIP users.

Quoted-string directives keep their escapes: the directive realm="the \"example\" value" becomes the Digest-Realm text the \"example\" value with length 23. Section 5 of the RFC also carries a table of which attributes may appear in which packets, and Section 6 gives worked examples.
sections.eli5: Each new slip has a number and a label such as realm, nonce or answer. Some slips may only go on certain forms, like only the "yes" form or only the "try again" form.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RADIUS inherits the weaknesses of HTTP Digest, plus its own. The new attributes are sent in cleartext, so a RADIUS client that accepts HTTPS or SIPS connections could expose information that the client meant to protect. An attacker who compromises a RADIUS client or proxy can mount a man-in-the-middle attack even when the other paths use TLS or IPsec. The RADIUS server MUST check Digest-Realm and treat a client not authorized for that realm as possibly compromised.

For denial of service, the server MUST check that it generated the nonce it receives, and SHOULD do so statelessly, for example with a random part plus a signature. Servers SHOULD include Digest-Qop and Digest-Algorithm in challenges, because a man in the middle can remove them in a bidding-down attack. Message-Authenticator MUST be included in all Access-Request, Challenge, Reject and Accept messages carrying these attributes.

Digest-HA1 has no random component for MD5 or AKAv1-MD5, which makes offline dictionary attacks easier and enables replay. When the HTTP-style client used TLS or IPsec, the RADIUS leg should be equally protected; the RFC suggests rejecting such requests or requiring IPsec to the RADIUS server.
sections.eli5: The phone line to head office is not private, so someone listening could pick up clues. The RFC says to use a private line when it matters, and to check that questions really came from head office.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 4590
sections.content:
RFC 5090 obsoletes RFC 4590. Its appendix lists the main changes. The table of attributes now shows that Digest-Method is required within an Access-Request, adds an entry for the State attribute and includes Accounting-Request messages.

The IANA section corrects two attribute assignment errors: Digest-Response-Auth is attribute 106 and Digest-Nextnonce is attribute 107. Several errors in the examples were also corrected.
sections.eli5: This is the corrected edition of an earlier book. Two label numbers and some worked examples had mistakes, and they were fixed.
